questions.q: The amount of work done to raise a mass '$m$' from the surface of the Earth to a height equal to the radius of the Earth '$R$', will be :
questions.solution:
Initial potential energy at the surface of the Earth is $U_i = -\dfrac{GMm}{R}$

Final potential energy at height $h = R$ is $U_f = -\dfrac{GMm}{R + R} = -\dfrac{GMm}{2R}$

Work done $W = \Delta U = U_f - U_i$

$W = -\dfrac{GMm}{2R} - \left(-\dfrac{GMm}{R}\right) = \dfrac{GMm}{2R}$

Using the relation $g = \dfrac{GM}{R^2}$, we get $GM = gR^2$

Substituting this in the expression for work done:

$W = \dfrac{gR^2 m}{2R} = mg\dfrac{R}{2}$

Answer: $mg\dfrac{R}{2}$

questions.q: Two planets $P_1$ and $P_2$ with equal mass have radii $R_1$ and $R_2$, respectively, where $R_2=\dfrac{R_1}{2}$. The escape speeds of $P_1$ and $P_2$ are $v_1$ and $v_2$, respectively. Then $\dfrac{v_2}{v_1}$ is :
questions.solution:
The escape speed of a planet of mass $M$ and radius $R$ is given by $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}}$.

For planet $P_1$, the escape speed is $v_1 = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R_1}}$.

For planet $P_2$, the escape speed is $v_2 = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R_2}}$.

Taking the ratio of the escape speeds:

$\dfrac{v_2}{v_1} = \sqrt{\dfrac{R_1}{R_2}}$

Given that $R_2 = \dfrac{R_1}{2}$, substituting this into the equation gives:

$\dfrac{v_2}{v_1} = \sqrt{\dfrac{R_1}{\dfrac{R_1}{2}}} = \sqrt{2}$

Answer: $\sqrt{2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In a solar system, the time-period of revolution of a planet tracing a circular orbit of radius R is proportional to :
questions.solution:
According to Kepler's third law of planetary motion, the square of the time period of revolution of a planet around the sun is directly proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis of its elliptical orbit.

For a circular orbit, the semi-major axis is equal to the radius of the orbit $R$.

Therefore, $T^2 \propto R^3$

Taking the square root on both sides, we get:

$T \propto R^{3/2}$

Alternatively, equating the gravitational force to the required centripetal force:

$\dfrac{GMm}{R^2} = \dfrac{mv^2}{R}$

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{R}}$

The time period $T$ is given by:

$T = \dfrac{2\pi R}{v} = \dfrac{2\pi R}{\sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{R}}} = \dfrac{2\pi}{\sqrt{GM}} R^{3/2}$

Thus, $T \propto R^{3/2}$.

Answer: $\text{R}^{3/2}$

questions.solution:
Let m be the mass of the satellite.

The potential energy of the satellite is 

U=-GMmr

The velocity of the satellite is given by 

v=GMr

Kinetic energy is given by

The total mechanical energy is the sum of potential and kinetic energy. So,

T=K+U=GMm2r-GMmr=-GMm2r

Hence, both the statements are false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements :

Statement-I: Acceleration due to gravity is different at different places on the surface of earth.

Statement-II: Acceleration due to gravity increases as we go down below the earth's surface.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questions.solution:
Acceleration due to gravity is the acceleration acquired by a freely falling object.

At any particular place on the Earth, the acceleration due to gravity depends on the latitude of the place and the angular frequency of Earth's rotation. Mathematically, the latitude dependence of acceleration due to gravity can be written as

geff= g-Rω2cos2λ.................(1)

where, geff is the effective acceleration due to gravity, g is the real value of gravity at the latitude without considering earth rotation, R is the radius of Earth, ω is the angular frequency of rotation and λ is the latitude of the place.

According to equation (1), the value of the acceleration due to gravity varies from place to place.

The variation of acceleration due to gravity with the depth can be written as

gd= g1-dR....................(2)

where, gd is the acceleration due to gravity at a depth d from the surface and g is the acceleration due to gravity at the surface.

From equation (2), it can be stated that the acceleration due to gravity decreases with the depth.

Hence, Statement I is true, but statement II is false.

Statement (B) The orbital velocity is inversely proportional to the square root of radius of the orbit.
Statement (C) The escape velocity of the body is independent of the altitude of the point of projection.
questions.solution:
Time period of satellite moving around a planet with angular velocity $\omega$ is given as,
$T=\frac{2 \pi}{\omega}$
Since, the two artificial satellites revolving in the same circular orbit, then their angular velocities will be same.
Hence, both satellites revolve with same period of revolution.
Orbital velocity of revolving satellite, $v=\sqrt{\frac{G m}{r}}$
i.e $v \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{r}}$
Where, $m=$ mass of the planet
$G=$ Universal gravitational constant
$r=$ radius of circular orbit.
Escape velocity depends on the gravitational potential at the point from where the body is launched. Since, this potential depends on the height of the point of projection, hence escape velocity also depends on the height (altitude) of the point of projection.

Newton's law of gravitation state that gravitational force between two point masses is directly proportional to the product of their masses m1 and m2 and inversely proportional to the square of the distance r between them. It is stated as F=Gm1m2r2

A planet moves around the sun in a circular path for which the gravitational force of attraction on the planet by the sun provides the necessary centripetal force. This centripetal force is always directed towards the centre of the sun at each point of its path which is responsible for circular motion of planet.

From Kepler's Third Law, we know that the squares of the orbital periods of the planets are directly proportional to the cubes of the semi-major axes of their orbits.

questions.q: Two satellites A and B are orbiting a planet in circular orbits. The time period of revolution of satellite B is 8 times that of satellite A. If the orbital radius of satellite A is $R$, what is the orbital radius of satellite B?
questions.solution:
According to Kepler's Third Law, the square of the time period is proportional to the cube of the orbital radius, i.e., $T^2 \propto r^3$.

This can be rearranged to find the radius dependence on the time period: $r \propto T^{2/3}$.

Taking the ratio for satellites B and A:
$\dfrac{r_B}{r_A} = \left(\dfrac{T_B}{T_A}\right)^{2/3}$

Given $T_B = 8 T_A$ and $r_A = R$:
$\dfrac{r_B}{R} = (8)^{2/3} = (2^3)^{2/3} = 2^2 = 4$

Therefore, $r_B = 4R$.

Answer: $4R$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A mass $m$ is moved from the bottom of a mine of depth $d = \dfrac{R}{2}$ to a height $h = \dfrac{R}{2}$ above the surface of the Earth. If $R$ is the radius of the Earth and $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity at its surface, the total work done in this process is:
questions.solution:
The gravitational potential energy of a mass $m$ at a distance $r$ from the centre of the Earth (where $r \lt R$) is given by:
$U = -\dfrac{GMm}{2R^3}(3R^2 - r^2)$

At a depth $d = \dfrac{R}{2}$, the distance from the centre is $r = R - \dfrac{R}{2} = \dfrac{R}{2}$.
Initial potential energy, $U_i = -\dfrac{GMm}{2R^3}\left(3R^2 - \left(\dfrac{R}{2}\right)^2\right) = -\dfrac{GMm}{2R^3}\left(3R^2 - \dfrac{R^2}{4}\right) = -\dfrac{11GMm}{8R}$

At a height $h = \dfrac{R}{2}$, the distance from the centre is $r = R + \dfrac{R}{2} = \dfrac{3R}{2}$.
Final potential energy, $U_f = -\dfrac{GMm}{r} = -\dfrac{GMm}{\dfrac{3R}{2}} = -\dfrac{2GMm}{3R}$

The total work done is the change in potential energy:
$W = U_f - U_i = -\dfrac{2GMm}{3R} - \left(-\dfrac{11GMm}{8R}\right) = \left(\dfrac{11}{8} - \dfrac{2}{3}\right)\dfrac{GMm}{R}$
$W = \left(\dfrac{33 - 16}{24}\right)\dfrac{GMm}{R} = \dfrac{17}{24}\dfrac{GMm}{R}$

Since $g = \dfrac{GM}{R^2}$, we have $\dfrac{GMm}{R} = mgR$.
Therefore, $W = \dfrac{17}{24} mgR$.

Answer: $\dfrac{17}{24} mgR$

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II. $R_E$ is the radius of the Earth.

List-IList-II
(A) Height above Earth's surface where weight of a body decreases by $75\%$(I) $\dfrac{R_E}{4}$
(B) Height above Earth's surface where weight of a body decreases by $36\%$(II) $\dfrac{3R_E}{4}$
(C) Depth below Earth's surface where weight of a body decreases by $75\%$(III) $\dfrac{9R_E}{25}$
(D) Depth below Earth's surface where weight of a body decreases by $36\%$(IV) $R_E$

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
Let the weight on the surface be $W = mg$.

For (A): Weight decreases by $75\%$, so it becomes $25\%$ of $W$.
$W_h = \dfrac{W}{4} \implies g_h = \dfrac{g}{4}$
Using $g_h = g\left(\dfrac{R_E}{R_E+h}\right)^2$, we get $\dfrac{1}{4} = \left(\dfrac{R_E}{R_E+h}\right)^2 \implies \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{R_E}{R_E+h} \implies h = R_E$. So, (A) matches (IV).

For (B): Weight decreases by $36\%$, so it becomes $64\%$ of $W$.
$W_h = \dfrac{16W}{25} \implies g_h = \dfrac{16g}{25}$
Using $g_h = g\left(\dfrac{R_E}{R_E+h}\right)^2$, we get $\dfrac{16}{25} = \left(\dfrac{R_E}{R_E+h}\right)^2 \implies \dfrac{4}{5} = \dfrac{R_E}{R_E+h} \implies 4R_E + 4h = 5R_E \implies h = \dfrac{R_E}{4}$. So, (B) matches (I).

For (C): Weight decreases by $75\%$, so it becomes $25\%$ of $W$.
$W_d = \dfrac{W}{4} \implies g_d = \dfrac{g}{4}$
Using $g_d = g\left(1 - \dfrac{d}{R_E}\right)$, we get $\dfrac{1}{4} = 1 - \dfrac{d}{R_E} \implies \dfrac{d}{R_E} = \dfrac{3}{4} \implies d = \dfrac{3R_E}{4}$. So, (C) matches (II).

For (D): Weight decreases by $36\%$, so it becomes $64\%$ of $W$.

Using $g_d = g\left(1 - \dfrac{d}{R_E}\right)$, we get $\dfrac{16}{25} = 1 - \dfrac{d}{R_E} \implies \dfrac{d}{R_E} = \dfrac{9}{25} \implies d = \dfrac{9R_E}{25}$. So, (D) matches (III).

Answer: (A)-(IV), (B)-(I), (C)-(II), (D)-(III)

questions.q: Two planets have escape velocities in the ratio $2 : 1$ and acceleration due to gravity at their surfaces in the ratio $1 : 2$. The ratio of their radii is:
questions.solution:
The escape velocity $v_e$ is related to the acceleration due to gravity $g$ and radius $R$ by the formula $v_e = \sqrt{2gR}$.

Rearranging this for the radius gives $R = \dfrac{v_e^2}{2g}$.

Therefore, the ratio of the radii of the two planets is:
$\dfrac{R_1}{R_2} = \left(\dfrac{v_1}{v_2}\right)^2 \times \left(\dfrac{g_2}{g_1}\right)$

Given $\dfrac{v_1}{v_2} = \dfrac{2}{1}$ and $\dfrac{g_1}{g_2} = \dfrac{1}{2}$ (which implies $\dfrac{g_2}{g_1} = \dfrac{2}{1}$):

$\dfrac{R_1}{R_2} = (2)^2 \times (2) = 4 \times 2 = 8$

The ratio of their radii is $8 : 1$.

Answer: $8 : 1$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A body is projected vertically upwards from the surface of the Earth with an initial velocity $v = \sqrt{gR}$, where $R$ is the radius of the Earth and $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity at the surface. The maximum height reached by the body from the surface of the Earth is:
questions.solution:
By the principle of conservation of mechanical energy, the loss in kinetic energy of the body equals its gain in gravitational potential energy.

The initial kinetic energy of the body is:

$K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}m(\sqrt{gR})^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}mgR$

The change in gravitational potential energy when the body reaches a maximum height $h$ is:

$\Delta U = \dfrac{mgh}{1 + \dfrac{h}{R}}$

Equating the loss in kinetic energy to the gain in potential energy:

$\dfrac{1}{2}mgR = \dfrac{mgh}{1 + \dfrac{h}{R}}$

Cancelling $mg$ from both sides:

$\dfrac{1}{2}R = \dfrac{hR}{R + h}$

Cross-multiplying yields:

$R + h = 2h$

$h = R$

Using the constant gravity approximation $mgh = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2$ would incorrectly give $h = \dfrac{R}{2}$.

Answer: $R$

Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): If a body is taken to a depth $d = \dfrac{R_E}{2}$, its weight becomes half of its weight on the surface, but if it is taken to a height $h = \dfrac{R_E}{2}$, its weight becomes less than half.
Reason (R): For a given distance from the surface of the Earth, the decrease in the value of acceleration due to gravity is always greater inside the Earth than outside it.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true.
questions.solution:
Let $g$ be the acceleration due to gravity on the surface of the Earth.

At depth $d = \dfrac{R_E}{2}$, the acceleration due to gravity is $g_d = g\left(1 - \dfrac{d}{R_E}\right) = g\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \dfrac{g}{2}$. Thus, the weight becomes half.

At height $h = \dfrac{R_E}{2}$, the acceleration due to gravity is $g_h = g\left(\dfrac{R_E}{R_E+h}\right)^2 = g\left(\dfrac{R_E}{R_E + R_E/2}\right)^2 = g\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^2 = \dfrac{4g}{9}$. Since $\dfrac{4}{9} \lt \dfrac{1}{2}$, the weight becomes less than half. Therefore, Assertion (A) is true.

The decrease in $g$ at depth $d = \dfrac{R_E}{2}$ is $\Delta g_{in} = g - \dfrac{g}{2} = \dfrac{g}{2} = 0.5g$.
The decrease in $g$ at height $h = \dfrac{R_E}{2}$ is $\Delta g_{out} = g - \dfrac{4g}{9} = \dfrac{5g}{9} \approx 0.55g$.
Since $\Delta g_{out} \gt \Delta g_{in}$, the decrease is greater outside the Earth than inside for the same distance from the surface. Therefore, Reason (R) is false.

Answer: Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.

The time period of a satellite in a circular orbit of radius $R$ around the Earth (mass $M$) is given by:

Therefore, two satellites of different masses ($m$ and $4m$) in the exact same orbit will have the same time period. Thus, Assertion (A) is true.

questions.q: Two planets revolve around a star in circular orbits. If the ratio of their orbital radii is $1:4$, what is the ratio of their average orbital speeds?
questions.solution:
The orbital speed $v$ of a planet in a circular orbit of radius $r$ is given by $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{r}}$, where $M$ is the mass of the star.

This implies that the orbital speed is inversely proportional to the square root of the orbital radius: $v \propto \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{r}}$.

Alternatively, using Kepler's Third Law ($T^2 \propto r^3$), the speed is $v = \dfrac{2\pi r}{T} \propto \dfrac{r}{r^{3/2}} = r^{-1/2}$.

Taking the ratio of the speeds of the two planets:
$\dfrac{v_1}{v_2} = \sqrt{\dfrac{r_2}{r_1}}$

Given the ratio of radii $\dfrac{r_1}{r_2} = \dfrac{1}{4}$, we have $\dfrac{r_2}{r_1} = \dfrac{4}{1}$.

$\dfrac{v_1}{v_2} = \sqrt{\dfrac{4}{1}} = \dfrac{2}{1}$

Thus, the ratio of their average orbital speeds is $2:1$.

Answer: $2:1$

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II regarding the acceleration due to gravity ($g$) at various positions relative to the earth's surface ($R$ is the radius of the earth).

List-IList-II
P. At a height $h = R$1. $g/9$
Q. At a height $h = 2R$2. $0$
R. At a depth $d = R/2$3. $g/4$
S. At a depth $d = R$4. $g/2$


Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
The acceleration due to gravity at a height $h$ is given by $g_h = \dfrac{g}{\left(1 + \dfrac{h}{R}\right)^2}$.

For P ($h = R$): $g_h = \dfrac{g}{\left(1 + 1\right)^2} = \dfrac{g}{4}$ (Matches with 3)

For Q ($h = 2R$): $g_h = \dfrac{g}{\left(1 + 2\right)^2} = \dfrac{g}{9}$ (Matches with 1)

The acceleration due to gravity at a depth $d$ is given by $g_d = g\left(1 - \dfrac{d}{R}\right)$.

For R ($d = \dfrac{R}{2}$): $g_d = g\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \dfrac{g}{2}$ (Matches with 4)

For S ($d = R$): $g_d = g\left(1 - 1\right) = 0$ (Matches with 2)

The correct matching is P-3, Q-1, R-4, S-2.

Answer: P-3, Q-1, R-4, S-2

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A satellite orbits the Earth with a time period of $24\text{ h}$ at an orbital radius $R$. Another satellite orbits the Earth with a time period of $3\text{ h}$. The orbital radius of the second satellite is:
questions.solution:
According to Kepler's third law of planetary motion, the square of the time period of a satellite is directly proportional to the cube of its orbital radius.

$T^2 \propto R^3$

For the two satellites, we can write the ratio as:

$\left(\dfrac{R_2}{R_1}\right)^3 = \left(\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}\right)^2$

Given that $T_1 = 24\text{ h}$, $R_1 = R$, and $T_2 = 3\text{ h}$:

$\left(\dfrac{R_2}{R}\right)^3 = \left(\dfrac{3}{24}\right)^2$

$\left(\dfrac{R_2}{R}\right)^3 = \left(\dfrac{1}{8}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{64}$

Taking the cube root on both sides:

$\dfrac{R_2}{R} = \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{1}{64}} = \dfrac{1}{4}$

$R_2 = \dfrac{R}{4}$

Answer: $\dfrac{R}{4}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An artificial satellite of mass $m$ is moved from an initial circular orbit at a height $R$ above the Earth's surface to a higher circular orbit at a height $3R$, where $R$ is the radius of the Earth. If $M$ is the mass of the Earth, the change in the gravitational potential energy of the satellite is:
questions.solution:
The distance of the initial orbit from the center of the Earth is $r_1 = R + R = 2R$.

The initial gravitational potential energy is $U_i = -\dfrac{GMm}{2R}$.

The distance of the final orbit from the center of the Earth is $r_2 = R + 3R = 4R$.

The final gravitational potential energy is $U_f = -\dfrac{GMm}{4R}$.

The change in gravitational potential energy is:
$\Delta U = U_f - U_i = -\dfrac{GMm}{4R} - \left(-\dfrac{GMm}{2R}\right) = \dfrac{GMm}{4R}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{GMm}{4R}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A body of mass '$m$' is raised from the surface of the Earth to various heights '$h$'. Match List-I (Height $h$) with List-II (Work done against gravity) and select the correct option.
(where '$R$' is the radius of the Earth and '$g$' is the acceleration due to gravity on the surface of the Earth)

List-IList-II
(A) $h = R$(I) $mgR$
(B) $h = 2R$(II) $mg\dfrac{R}{2}$
(C) $h = 3R$(III) $\dfrac{2}{3}mgR$
(D) $h \rightarrow \infty$(IV) $\dfrac{3}{4}mgR$
questions.solution:
The work done in raising a mass $m$ from the surface of the Earth to a height $h$ is equal to the change in its gravitational potential energy.

Initial potential energy at the surface, $U_i = -\dfrac{GMm}{R}$.
Final potential energy at height $h$, $U_f = -\dfrac{GMm}{R+h}$.

Work done, $W = U_f - U_i = \dfrac{GMm}{R} - \dfrac{GMm}{R+h} = \dfrac{GMmh}{R(R+h)}$.
Using $GM = gR^2$, we get $W = \dfrac{mgh}{1 + \dfrac{h}{R}}$.

For (A) $h = R$: $W = \dfrac{mgR}{1 + 1} = mg\dfrac{R}{2}$. (Matches II)

For (B) $h = 2R$: $W = \dfrac{mg(2R)}{1 + 2} = \dfrac{2}{3}mgR$. (Matches III)

For (C) $h = 3R$: $W = \dfrac{mg(3R)}{1 + 3} = \dfrac{3}{4}mgR$. (Matches IV)

For (D) $h \rightarrow \infty$: $W = \lim_{h \to \infty} \dfrac{mgh}{1 + \dfrac{h}{R}} = mgR$. (Matches I)

Therefore, the correct matching is (A) - (II), (B) - (III), (C) - (IV), (D) - (I).

Answer: (A) - (II), (B) - (III), (C) - (IV), (D) - (I)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
The mass and radius of four hypothetical planets A, B, C and D are given below in terms of the mass ($M$) and radius ($R$) of the Earth:
Planet A: Mass $M$, Radius $R$
Planet B: Mass $2M$, Radius $R/2$
Planet C: Mass $4M$, Radius $2R$
Planet D: Mass $8M$, Radius $4R$

Which of these planets has the highest escape velocity for an object on its surface?
questions.solution:
The escape velocity of a planet is given by $v_e = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}}$, which means $v_e \propto \sqrt{\dfrac{M}{R}}$.

Calculating the ratio $\dfrac{M}{R}$ for each planet:
For Planet A: $\dfrac{M}{R} = 1$
For Planet B: $\dfrac{2M}{R/2} = 4$
For Planet C: $\dfrac{4M}{2R} = 2$
For Planet D: $\dfrac{8M}{4R} = 2$

Since Planet B has the highest value of the ratio $\dfrac{M}{R}$, it yields the highest value for $\sqrt{\dfrac{M}{R}}$ and thus the highest escape velocity.

Answer: Planet B

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An object is raised from the surface of the Earth (radius $R$) to a height $h_1 = R$, requiring work $W_1$. The same object is raised from the surface of the Earth to a height $h_2 = 2R$, requiring work $W_2$. The ratio $W_1 : W_2$ is
questions.solution:
The work done in raising an object from the surface of the Earth to a height $h$ is given by the change in gravitational potential energy:

$W = \Delta U = -\dfrac{GMm}{R+h} - \left(-\dfrac{GMm}{R}\right) = \dfrac{GMmh}{R(R+h)}$

For $h_1 = R$:

$W_1 = \dfrac{GMm(R)}{R(R+R)} = \dfrac{GMm}{2R}$

For $h_2 = 2R$:

$W_2 = \dfrac{GMm(2R)}{R(R+2R)} = \dfrac{2GMm}{3R}$

The ratio of the work done is:

$\dfrac{W_1}{W_2} = \dfrac{\dfrac{GMm}{2R}}{\dfrac{2GMm}{3R}} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{3}{2} = \dfrac{3}{4}$

Thus, the ratio $W_1 : W_2$ is $3 : 4$.

Answer: $3 : 4$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): If a body is projected from the earth's surface at an angle of $45^{\circ}$ to the vertical, its escape velocity remains the same as when projected vertically upwards.

Reason (R): Escape velocity depends only on the mass and radius of the planet and is independent of the mass of the body and the angle of projection.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are correct but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is correct but Reason (R) is incorrect.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are correct and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is incorrect but Reason (R) is correct.
questions.solution:
The escape velocity of a body from the surface of a planet is given by $v_e = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}}$, where $M$ is the mass of the planet and $R$ is its radius.

This expression is derived using the principle of conservation of mechanical energy. Since kinetic and potential energies are scalar quantities, the escape velocity is independent of the angle of projection and the direction in which the body is thrown.

The formula also shows that $v_e$ is independent of the mass of the projected body. Thus, both the Assertion and the Reason are correct, and the Reason correctly explains why the escape velocity remains the same regardless of the angle of projection.

Answer: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are correct and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A satellite A revolves around a planet of radius $R$ at a height $R$ from its surface. Its time period of revolution is $T$. Another satellite B revolves around the same planet with a time period of $8T$. What is the height of satellite B from the surface of the planet?
questions.solution:
According to Kepler's third law, the square of the time period is proportional to the cube of the orbital radius: $T^2 \propto r^3$, which gives $T \propto r^{3/2}$.

Let $r_A$ and $r_B$ be the orbital radii of satellites A and B respectively.
The orbital radius of satellite A is $r_A = R + h_A = R + R = 2R$.

Taking the ratio of their time periods:
$\dfrac{T_B}{T_A} = \left(\dfrac{r_B}{r_A}\right)^{3/2}$

Given $T_A = T$ and $T_B = 8T$:
$\dfrac{8T}{T} = \left(\dfrac{r_B}{2R}\right)^{3/2}$

$8 = \left(\dfrac{r_B}{2R}\right)^{3/2}$

Raising both sides to the power of $2/3$:
$\dfrac{r_B}{2R} = (8)^{2/3} = 4$

$r_B = 4 \times 2R = 8R$

The height of satellite B from the surface is:
$h_B = r_B - R = 8R - R = 7R$.

Answer: $7R$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two point masses $M$ and $16M$ are fixed at a separation distance of $10a$. A small particle is released from rest at the point on the line joining them where the net gravitational field is zero. What is the minimum speed the particle must be given at this point so that it escapes to infinity?
questions.solution:
Let the neutral point be at a distance $x$ from the mass $M$.

Equating the magnitudes of the gravitational fields due to both masses:
$\dfrac{GM}{x^2} = \dfrac{G(16M)}{(10a-x)^2}$

Taking the square root on both sides:
$\dfrac{1}{x} = \dfrac{4}{10a-x}$
$\Rightarrow 10a - x = 4x \Rightarrow 5x = 10a \Rightarrow x = 2a$

The distance of this neutral point from the mass $16M$ is $10a - 2a = 8a$.

The net gravitational potential $V$ at this neutral point is:
$V = -\dfrac{GM}{2a} - \dfrac{G(16M)}{8a}$
$V = -\dfrac{GM}{2a} - \dfrac{2GM}{a} = -\dfrac{5GM}{2a}$

To escape to infinity, the total mechanical energy of the particle must be at least zero. By conservation of mechanical energy:
$\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + mV = 0$
$\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + m\left(-\dfrac{5GM}{2a}\right) = 0$
$\dfrac{1}{2}v^2 = \dfrac{5GM}{2a}$
$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{5GM}{a}}$

Answer: $\sqrt{\dfrac{5GM}{a}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A space probe is to be launched from the surface of a planet such that it retains a speed equal to the escape velocity ($v_e$) of the planet when it reaches interstellar space (at an infinite distance). What must be the initial projection speed of the probe from the surface of the planet?
questions.solution:
By the principle of conservation of mechanical energy, the total energy at the surface of the planet equals the total energy at infinity.

$K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f$

$\dfrac{1}{2}mv_p^2 - \dfrac{GMm}{R} = \dfrac{1}{2}mv_{\infty}^2 + 0$

Since the escape velocity from the surface is $v_e = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}}$, we can write $\dfrac{GMm}{R} = \dfrac{1}{2}mv_e^2$.

Substituting this into the energy equation:

$\dfrac{1}{2}mv_p^2 - \dfrac{1}{2}mv_e^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}mv_{\infty}^2$

$v_p^2 - v_e^2 = v_{\infty}^2$

It is given that the desired velocity at infinity is $v_{\infty} = v_e$. Substituting this value:

$v_p^2 - v_e^2 = v_e^2$

$v_p^2 = 2v_e^2$

$v_p = \sqrt{2}v_e$

A common mistake is to add the velocities linearly ($v_p = v_{\infty} + v_e = 2v_e$), which ignores the quadratic nature of kinetic energy.

Answer: $\sqrt{2}v_e$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A graph is plotted between the logarithm of the time period of revolution ($\log \mathrm{T}$) on the y-axis and the logarithm of the semi-major axis ($\log \mathrm{r}$) on the x-axis for various planets orbiting the Sun. The slope of the resulting straight line will be
questions.solution:
According to Kepler's third law of planetary motion, the square of the time period of revolution ($\mathrm{T}$) is directly proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis ($\mathrm{r}$) of the orbit.

$\mathrm{T}^2 \propto \mathrm{r}^3$

$\mathrm{T}^2 = \mathrm{K} \mathrm{r}^3$

Taking logarithm on both sides, we get:

$2 \log \mathrm{T} = 3 \log \mathrm{r} + \log \mathrm{K}$

$\log \mathrm{T} = \dfrac{3}{2} \log \mathrm{r} + \dfrac{1}{2} \log \mathrm{K}$

Comparing this with the equation of a straight line, $y = mx + c$, where $y = \log \mathrm{T}$ and $x = \log \mathrm{r}$, the slope $m$ is given by:

$m = \dfrac{3}{2}$

Answer: $\dfrac{3}{2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A body is projected vertically upwards from the surface of the Earth with an initial velocity equal to half of the escape velocity. The maximum height attained by the body from the surface of the Earth will be :
(where '$R$' is the radius of the Earth)
questions.solution:
Let the mass of the body be $m$ and the mass of the Earth be $M$.

The escape velocity from the surface of the Earth is $v_e = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}}$.

Initial velocity of the body, $v = \dfrac{v_e}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{2R}}$.

By the principle of conservation of mechanical energy:

Initial Total Energy = Final Total Energy

$K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f$

$\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 - \dfrac{GMm}{R} = 0 - \dfrac{GMm}{R+h}$

$\dfrac{1}{2}m\left(\dfrac{GM}{2R}\right) - \dfrac{GMm}{R} = -\dfrac{GMm}{R+h}$

$\dfrac{GMm}{4R} - \dfrac{GMm}{R} = -\dfrac{GMm}{R+h}$

$-\dfrac{3GMm}{4R} = -\dfrac{GMm}{R+h}$

$\dfrac{3}{4R} = \dfrac{1}{R+h}$

$3R + 3h = 4R$

$3h = R \Rightarrow h = \dfrac{R}{3}$

Answer: $\dfrac{R}{3}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A space probe is launched from the surface of the Earth with a speed equal to $1.5$ times the escape velocity ($V_e$). The residual speed of the probe when it reaches interstellar space (very far away from the Earth) is
questions.solution:
Let the mass of the Earth be $M$, radius be $R$, and mass of the probe be $m$.

By conservation of mechanical energy between the surface of the Earth and infinity:
$K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f$

At the surface, the velocity is $v = 1.5 V_e$. At infinity, the potential energy is zero and the velocity is $v_{\infty}$.

$\dfrac{1}{2}m(1.5 V_e)^2 - \dfrac{GMm}{R} = \dfrac{1}{2}mv_{\infty}^2 + 0$

We know that the escape velocity $V_e = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}}$, which gives $\dfrac{GM}{R} = \dfrac{V_e^2}{2}$.

Substituting this into the energy equation:
$\dfrac{1}{2} (2.25 V_e^2) - \dfrac{1}{2} V_e^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} v_{\infty}^2$

Multiplying the entire equation by $2$:
$2.25 V_e^2 - V_e^2 = v_{\infty}^2$

$1.25 V_e^2 = v_{\infty}^2$

$v_{\infty} = \sqrt{1.25} V_e = \sqrt{\dfrac{5}{4}} V_e = \dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{2} V_e$

Answer: $\dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{2} V_e$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An object is released from a height $h_1 = 3R_E$ above the surface of the earth, where $R_E$ is the radius of the earth. As it falls, it reaches a height $h_2$ above the earth's surface where its weight becomes $4$ times its weight at the release point. The value of $h_2$ is:
questions.solution:
The acceleration due to gravity at a height $h$ from the surface of the earth is given by $g_h = g \left(\dfrac{R_E}{R_E + h}\right)^2$.

At the initial height $h_1 = 3R_E$, the acceleration due to gravity is:
$g_1 = g \left(\dfrac{R_E}{R_E + 3R_E}\right)^2 = g \left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^2 = \dfrac{g}{16}$

The weight of the object at this height is $W_1 = m g_1 = \dfrac{mg}{16}$.

At height $h_2$, the weight becomes $4$ times the initial weight:
$W_2 = 4 W_1 = 4 \times \dfrac{mg}{16} = \dfrac{mg}{4}$

This means the acceleration due to gravity at $h_2$ is $g_2 = \dfrac{g}{4}$.

Using the formula for $g$ at height $h_2$:
$\dfrac{g}{4} = g \left(\dfrac{R_E}{R_E + h_2}\right)^2$

Taking the square root on both sides:
$\dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{R_E}{R_E + h_2}$

$R_E + h_2 = 2R_E$

$h_2 = R_E$

Thus, the height $h_2$ is $R_E$.

Answer: $R_E$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A body of mass $m$ is released from rest from a height $h = 2R$ above the surface of the Earth, where $R$ is the radius of the Earth and $M$ is its mass. The kinetic energy of the body just before it strikes the Earth's surface is:
questions.solution:
According to the principle of conservation of mechanical energy, the total energy of the body remains constant.

Initial kinetic energy, $K_i = 0$.
Initial distance from the center of the Earth, $r_1 = R + 2R = 3R$.
Initial potential energy, $U_i = -\dfrac{GMm}{3R}$.

Final distance from the center of the Earth (at the surface), $r_2 = R$.
Final potential energy, $U_f = -\dfrac{GMm}{R}$.

Let the final kinetic energy be $K_f$. Applying conservation of energy:
$K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f$
$0 - \dfrac{GMm}{3R} = K_f - \dfrac{GMm}{R}$
$K_f = \dfrac{GMm}{R} - \dfrac{GMm}{3R} = \dfrac{2GMm}{3R}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{2GMm}{3R}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A body of mass '$m$' is raised vertically from the surface of the Earth. If the work done against gravity is $\dfrac{3}{4}mgR$, where '$g$' is the acceleration due to gravity at the surface and '$R$' is the radius of the Earth, the height attained by the body is :
questions.solution:
The work done against gravity in raising a mass $m$ to a height $h$ from the Earth's surface is given by the change in gravitational potential energy.

Initial potential energy, $U_i = -\dfrac{GMm}{R}$

Final potential energy, $U_f = -\dfrac{GMm}{R+h}$

Work done, $W = U_f - U_i = \dfrac{GMm}{R} - \dfrac{GMm}{R+h} = \dfrac{GMmh}{R(R+h)}$

Using $GM = gR^2$, we get:

$W = \dfrac{mgh}{1 + \dfrac{h}{R}}$

Given that $W = \dfrac{3}{4}mgR$, we equate the two expressions:

$\dfrac{mgh}{1 + \dfrac{h}{R}} = \dfrac{3}{4}mgR$

$\dfrac{h}{1 + \dfrac{h}{R}} = \dfrac{3}{4}R$

$4h = 3R \left(1 + \dfrac{h}{R}\right)$

$4h = 3R + 3h$

$h = 3R$

Answer: $3R$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A body is taken from the bottom of a deep mine of depth $d = \dfrac{R_E}{2}$ to a height $h$ above the surface of the earth, where $R_E$ is the radius of the earth. If the weight of the body is found to be the same at both these locations, the value of $h$ is:
questions.solution:
The acceleration due to gravity at a depth $d$ is given by $g_d = g \left(1 - \dfrac{d}{R_E}\right)$.

At a depth $d = \dfrac{R_E}{2}$, the value of $g$ is:
$g_d = g \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \dfrac{g}{2}$

The acceleration due to gravity at a height $h$ (comparable to $R_E$) is given by $g_h = g \left(\dfrac{R_E}{R_E + h}\right)^2$.

Since the weight of the body is the same at both locations, the acceleration due to gravity must be equal ($g_d = g_h$):
$\dfrac{g}{2} = g \left(\dfrac{R_E}{R_E + h}\right)^2$

$\dfrac{1}{2} = \left(\dfrac{R_E}{R_E + h}\right)^2$

Taking the square root on both sides:
$\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{R_E}{R_E + h}$

$R_E + h = \sqrt{2}R_E$

$h = (\sqrt{2} - 1)R_E$

Thus, the height $h$ is $(\sqrt{2} - 1)R_E$.

Answer: $(\sqrt{2} - 1)R_E$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: At what height above the surface of the earth will the weight of a body become $64\%$ of its weight on the surface of the earth? (where $R$ is the radius of the earth)
questions.solution:
Let the weight of the body on the surface of the earth be $W = mg$.

The weight at a height $h$ is given by $W_h = \dfrac{W}{\left(1 + \dfrac{h}{R}\right)^2}$.

Given that $W_h = 64\%$ of $W = 0.64 W$.

Equating the two expressions:
$0.64 W = \dfrac{W}{\left(1 + \dfrac{h}{R}\right)^2}$

$\left(1 + \dfrac{h}{R}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{0.64} = \dfrac{100}{64} = \dfrac{25}{16}$

Taking the square root on both sides:
$1 + \dfrac{h}{R} = \dfrac{5}{4}$

$\dfrac{h}{R} = \dfrac{5}{4} - 1 = \dfrac{1}{4}$

$h = \dfrac{R}{4}$

Using the approximate formula $W_h = W\left(1 - \dfrac{2h}{R}\right)$ leads to the incorrect answer $\dfrac{9R}{50}$, as the approximation is only valid for $h \ll R$.

Answer: $\dfrac{R}{4}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A planet of mass $81M$ and its moon of mass $M$ are separated by a distance $10d$. A spaceship of mass $m$ is parked on the line joining them at a point where the net gravitational force on it is zero. What is the gravitational potential energy of the spaceship at this position?
questions.solution:
Let the spaceship be at a distance $x$ from the planet. The net gravitational force on it is zero, so the gravitational fields of the planet and the moon must be equal in magnitude at this point.

$\dfrac{G(81M)m}{x^2} = \dfrac{GMm}{(10d - x)^2}$

Taking the square root of both sides:
$\dfrac{9}{x} = \dfrac{1}{10d - x}$

$\Rightarrow 90d - 9x = x$
$\Rightarrow 10x = 90d \Rightarrow x = 9d$

The spaceship is at a distance of $9d$ from the planet and $10d - 9d = d$ from the moon.

The gravitational potential energy $U$ of the spaceship is the scalar sum of the potential energies due to both bodies:
$U = -\dfrac{G(81M)m}{9d} - \dfrac{GMm}{d}$

$U = -\dfrac{9GMm}{d} - \dfrac{GMm}{d} = -\dfrac{10GMm}{d}$

Answer: $-\dfrac{10GMm}{d}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): If a body is projected from the earth's surface with a speed of $3v_e$ (where $v_e$ is the escape velocity), its speed at interstellar distance (infinity) is $2\sqrt{2}v_e$.
Reason (R): For a body projected with a speed $v \gt v_e$, its speed at infinity is not given by the linear difference $(v - v_e)$.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Assertion is false but Reason is true.
questions.solution:
Assertion (A) is true: By the conservation of mechanical energy, the velocity of a body at infinity ($v_{\infty}$) when projected with a velocity $v$ is given by $v_{\infty} = \sqrt{v^2 - v_e^2}$.
Substituting $v = 3v_e$:
$v_{\infty} = \sqrt{(3v_e)^2 - v_e^2} = \sqrt{9v_e^2 - v_e^2} = \sqrt{8v_e^2} = 2\sqrt{2}v_e$.

Reason (R) is true: The speed at infinity is indeed not calculated by the linear subtraction $v - v_e$. A common misconception is to write $v_{\infty} = 3v_e - v_e = 2v_e$, which is incorrect.

However, Reason (R) is merely a negative statement pointing out that the linear formula is wrong. It does not state the actual principle (conservation of energy) or the correct quadratic formula ($v_{\infty}^2 = v^2 - v_e^2$) required to derive the value $2\sqrt{2}v_e$. Therefore, while both statements are true, Reason (R) is not the correct explanation for Assertion (A).

Answer: Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A satellite of mass '$m$' is revolving in a circular orbit around the Earth at a height '$R$' from the surface of the Earth. The minimum energy required to transfer the satellite into a higher circular orbit at a height '$3R$' from the surface of the Earth is :
(where '$R$' is the radius of the Earth and '$g$' is the acceleration due to gravity on the surface of the Earth)
questions.solution:
For a satellite orbiting the Earth at a distance $r$ from its centre, the total energy is given by $E = -\dfrac{GMm}{2r}$.

Initial distance from the centre of the Earth, $r_1 = R + R = 2R$.
Initial total energy, $E_1 = -\dfrac{GMm}{2(2R)} = -\dfrac{GMm}{4R}$.

Final distance from the centre of the Earth, $r_2 = R + 3R = 4R$.
Final total energy, $E_2 = -\dfrac{GMm}{2(4R)} = -\dfrac{GMm}{8R}$.

Minimum energy required to shift the satellite, $\Delta E = E_2 - E_1$
$\Delta E = -\dfrac{GMm}{8R} - \left(-\dfrac{GMm}{4R}\right) = \dfrac{GMm}{8R}$.

Using the relation $g = \dfrac{GM}{R^2}$, we get $GM = gR^2$.

Substituting this value, the energy required is:
$\Delta E = \dfrac{gR^2 m}{8R} = mg\dfrac{R}{8}$.

Note: Calculating only the change in potential energy gives $mg\dfrac{R}{4}$, and forgetting to add the Earth's radius to the heights gives $mg\dfrac{R}{3}$.

Answer: $mg\dfrac{R}{8}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle is projected vertically upwards from the surface of the earth with a speed equal to one-half of the escape velocity. What is the maximum height attained by the particle? (Let $R$ be the radius of the earth)
questions.solution:
Let the mass of the earth be $M$ and its radius be $R$. The escape velocity from the surface of the earth is given by $v_e = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}}$.

The initial speed of the particle is $v = \dfrac{v_e}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}}$.

By the principle of conservation of mechanical energy:
$K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f$

$\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 - \dfrac{GMm}{R} = 0 - \dfrac{GMm}{R+h}$

Substituting the value of $v$:
$\dfrac{1}{2}m\left(\dfrac{1}{4} \times \dfrac{2GM}{R}\right) - \dfrac{GMm}{R} = -\dfrac{GMm}{R+h}$

$\dfrac{GMm}{4R} - \dfrac{GMm}{R} = -\dfrac{GMm}{R+h}$

$-\dfrac{3GMm}{4R} = -\dfrac{GMm}{R+h}$

$\dfrac{3}{4R} = \dfrac{1}{R+h}$

$3(R+h) = 4R$

$3R + 3h = 4R \implies 3h = R \implies h = \dfrac{R}{3}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{R}{3}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The escape velocity on the surface of planet $A$ is $4$ times the escape velocity on the surface of planet $B$. If the mass of planet $A$ is $8$ times the mass of planet $B$, then the ratio of their radii $\left(\dfrac{R_A}{R_B}\right)$ is :
questions.solution:
The escape velocity of a planet is given by $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}}$.

Taking the ratio of the escape velocities for planets $A$ and $B$:

$\dfrac{v_A}{v_B} = \sqrt{\dfrac{M_A}{M_B} \times \dfrac{R_B}{R_A}}$

We are given that $\dfrac{v_A}{v_B} = 4$ and $\dfrac{M_A}{M_B} = 8$. Substituting these values into the equation gives:

$4 = \sqrt{8 \times \dfrac{R_B}{R_A}}$

Squaring both sides:

$16 = 8 \times \dfrac{R_B}{R_A}$

$\dfrac{R_B}{R_A} = \dfrac{16}{8} = 2$

Therefore, the ratio of their radii is:

$\dfrac{R_A}{R_B} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The work required to move a body of mass $m$ from the surface of the Earth (radius $R$) to infinity is $W$. The work required to move the same body from the surface of the Earth to a height $h = R$ above the surface is
questions.solution:
The work done to move a body from the surface of the Earth to infinity is equal to the change in its gravitational potential energy:

$W = U_{\infty} - U_{\text{surface}} = 0 - \left(-\dfrac{GMm}{R}\right) = \dfrac{GMm}{R}$

The work done to move the body from the surface to a height $h = R$ is:

$W' = U_{\text{final}} - U_{\text{initial}} = -\dfrac{GMm}{R+R} - \left(-\dfrac{GMm}{R}\right)$

$W' = -\dfrac{GMm}{2R} + \dfrac{GMm}{R} = \dfrac{GMm}{2R}$

Comparing the two expressions, we get:

$W' = \dfrac{1}{2} \left(\dfrac{GMm}{R}\right) = \dfrac{W}{2}$

Answer: $\dfrac{W}{2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two satellites A and B are revolving around a planet in coplanar circular orbits. If the radius of satellite B's orbit is $4$ times the radius of satellite A's orbit, what is the ratio of their time periods ($T_A : T_B$)?
questions.solution:
According to Kepler's third law of planetary motion, the square of the time period of revolution is proportional to the cube of the orbital radius:

$T^2 \propto R^3$

Taking the square root on both sides, we get:

$T \propto R^{3/2}$

Let the radius of satellite A's orbit be $R_A = R$. Then the radius of satellite B's orbit is $R_B = 4R$.

The ratio of their time periods is:

$\dfrac{T_A}{T_B} = \left(\dfrac{R_A}{R_B}\right)^{3/2} = \left(\dfrac{R}{4R}\right)^{3/2} = \left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^{3/2}$

Since $\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^{1/2} = \dfrac{1}{2}$, cubing this gives:

$\dfrac{T_A}{T_B} = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^3 = \dfrac{1}{8}$

Thus, the ratio of their time periods is $1 : 8$.

Answer: $1 : 8$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A body is projected radially outwards from a height $h = R$ above the surface of the Earth, where $R$ is the radius of the Earth. If the body is projected with a speed equal to the escape velocity of the Earth's surface ($v_e$), what will be its speed at an infinite distance from the Earth?
questions.solution:
Let the mass of the Earth be $M$ and the mass of the body be $m$.

The escape velocity at the surface of the Earth is $v_e = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}}$, which gives $\dfrac{GM}{R} = \dfrac{v_e^2}{2}$.

The body is projected from a height $h = R$, so its initial distance from the centre of the Earth is $r = R + h = 2R$.

Initial potential energy, $U_i = -\dfrac{GMm}{2R} = -\dfrac{1}{2}m\left(\dfrac{GM}{R}\right) = -\dfrac{1}{4}mv_e^2$.

Initial kinetic energy, $K_i = \dfrac{1}{2}mv_p^2$. Since $v_p = v_e$, $K_i = \dfrac{1}{2}mv_e^2$.

Total initial energy, $E_i = K_i + U_i = \dfrac{1}{2}mv_e^2 - \dfrac{1}{4}mv_e^2 = \dfrac{1}{4}mv_e^2$.

At infinity, the potential energy $U_f = 0$, and the kinetic energy is $K_f = \dfrac{1}{2}mv_{\infty}^2$.

By conservation of mechanical energy, $E_i = E_f$:

$\dfrac{1}{4}mv_e^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}mv_{\infty}^2$

$v_{\infty}^2 = \dfrac{v_e^2}{2}$

$v_{\infty} = \dfrac{v_e}{\sqrt{2}}$

Answer: $\dfrac{v_e}{\sqrt{2}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Planet A has a radius $R$, uniform density $d$, and an escape velocity $v_e$ from its surface. Planet B has a radius $2R$ and the same uniform density $d$. If a body is projected from the surface of Planet B with a velocity of $3v_e$, what will be the velocity of this body at an infinite distance from Planet B?
questions.solution:
The escape velocity from the surface of a planet of radius $R$ and uniform density $d$ is given by:
$v_e = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2G}{R} \left(\dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^3 d\right)} = R \sqrt{\dfrac{8}{3}\pi G d}$

Since density is constant, the escape velocity is directly proportional to the radius of the planet ($v_e \propto R$).
For Planet B, the radius is $2R$, so its escape velocity is $v_{eB} = 2v_e$.

By the principle of conservation of mechanical energy for the body projected from Planet B:
$\dfrac{1}{2} m v_{proj}^2 - \dfrac{GM_B m}{R_B} = \dfrac{1}{2} m v_{\infty}^2 + 0$
$v_{\infty}^2 = v_{proj}^2 - v_{eB}^2$

Substitute $v_{proj} = 3v_e$ and $v_{eB} = 2v_e$:
$v_{\infty}^2 = (3v_e)^2 - (2v_e)^2$
$v_{\infty}^2 = 9v_e^2 - 4v_e^2 = 5v_e^2$

$v_{\infty} = \sqrt{5} v_e$

Answer: $\sqrt{5} v_e$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The work done to raise a body of mass $m$ from the surface of the Earth to a certain height $h$ is $\dfrac{3}{4}mgR$, where $R$ is the radius of the Earth and $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity at the surface. The height $h$ is:
questions.solution:
The change in gravitational potential energy when a mass $m$ is raised to a height $h$ from the Earth's surface is given by:

$W = \Delta U = \dfrac{mgh}{1 + \dfrac{h}{R}}$

Given that the work done is $W = \dfrac{3}{4}mgR$, we can equate the two expressions:

$\dfrac{3}{4}mgR = \dfrac{mgh}{1 + \dfrac{h}{R}}$

Cancelling $mg$ from both sides:

$\dfrac{3}{4}R = \dfrac{h}{1 + \dfrac{h}{R}}$

$\dfrac{3}{4}R = \dfrac{hR}{R + h}$

Cross-multiplying gives:

$3(R + h) = 4h$

$3R + 3h = 4h$

$h = 3R$

Using the incorrect approximation $W = mgh$ would lead to the wrong answer $h = \dfrac{3}{4}R$.

Answer: $3R$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): If the distance of the Earth from the Sun were suddenly reduced to half its present value, the number of days in a year would become approximately $129$.

Reason (R): The time period of revolution of a planet is directly proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis of its elliptical orbit.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
questions.solution:
Assertion (A) is true: Let the initial distance be $\mathrm{r}_1 = \mathrm{r}$ and initial time period be $\mathrm{T}_1 = 365$ days.

If the distance is reduced to half, $\mathrm{r}_2 = \dfrac{\mathrm{r}}{2}$.

According to Kepler's third law, $\mathrm{T}^2 \propto \mathrm{r}^3$.

$\left(\dfrac{\mathrm{T}_2}{\mathrm{T}_1}\right)^2 = \left(\dfrac{\mathrm{r}_2}{\mathrm{r}_1}\right)^3$

$\dfrac{\mathrm{T}_2}{365} = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{3/2} = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}$

$\mathrm{T}_2 = \dfrac{365}{2 \times 1.414} \approx \dfrac{365}{2.828} \approx 129$ days.

Reason (R) is false: Kepler's third law states that the square of the time period of revolution ($\mathrm{T}^2$) is directly proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis ($\mathrm{r}^3$), not the time period itself.

Therefore, (A) is true but (R) is false.

Answer: (A) is true but (R) is false

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The weight of a body at a height $h = \dfrac{R}{3}$ above the surface of the earth is equal to its weight at a depth $d$ below the surface of the earth. If $R$ is the radius of the earth, what is the value of $d$?
questions.solution:
The acceleration due to gravity at a height $h = \dfrac{R}{3}$ is given by the exact formula:
$g_h = \dfrac{g}{\left(1 + \dfrac{h}{R}\right)^2}$

Substituting $h = \dfrac{R}{3}$:
$g_h = \dfrac{g}{\left(1 + \dfrac{1}{3}\right)^2} = \dfrac{g}{\left(\dfrac{4}{3}\right)^2} = \dfrac{9g}{16}$

The acceleration due to gravity at a depth $d$ is given by:
$g_d = g\left(1 - \dfrac{d}{R}\right)$

Since the weight of the body is the same at both positions, $g_h = g_d$:
$\dfrac{9g}{16} = g\left(1 - \dfrac{d}{R}\right)$

$1 - \dfrac{d}{R} = \dfrac{9}{16}$

$\dfrac{d}{R} = 1 - \dfrac{9}{16} = \dfrac{7}{16}$

$d = \dfrac{7R}{16}$

Using the approximate formula for height $g_h = g\left(1 - \dfrac{2h}{R}\right)$ incorrectly yields $d = \dfrac{2R}{3}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{7R}{16}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A satellite is orbiting very close to the surface of a spherical planet of uniform density $\rho$. The time period of revolution of this satellite is proportional to:
questions.solution:
For a satellite orbiting very close to the surface of a planet, the orbital radius is approximately equal to the radius of the planet $R$.

The time period $T$ of the satellite is given by:

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{R^3}{GM}}$

The mass $M$ of the spherical planet of uniform density $\rho$ is:

$M = \text{Volume} \times \text{Density} = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^3 \rho$

Substituting the expression for $M$ into the time period formula:

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{R^3}{G \left(\dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^3 \rho\right)}}$

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{3}{4\pi G \rho}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3\pi}{G \rho}}$

Since $G$ and $\pi$ are constants, the time period $T$ depends only on the density $\rho$ as:

$T \propto \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\rho}} \Rightarrow T \propto \rho^{-1/2}$

Answer: $\rho^{-1/2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Match the hypothetical planets in List-I (with given mass and radius in terms of Earth's mass $M$ and radius $R$) with their corresponding escape velocities in List-II (in terms of Earth's escape velocity $v_e$).

List-IList-II
(A) Mass $2M$, Radius $\dfrac{R}{2}$(I) $v_e$
(B) Mass $\dfrac{M}{2}$, Radius $2R$(II) $\dfrac{v_e}{2}$
(C) Mass $2M$, Radius $2R$(III) $2v_e$
(D) Mass $4M$, Radius $\dfrac{R}{4}$(IV) $4v_e$

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
The escape velocity on the surface of a planet of mass $M$ and radius $R$ is given by $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}}$.

For Earth, $v_e = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}}$.

For planet (A): Mass $= 2M$, Radius $= \dfrac{R}{2}$
$v_A = \sqrt{\dfrac{2G(2M)}{\dfrac{R}{2}}} = \sqrt{4 \times \dfrac{2GM}{R}} = 2v_e$. (Matches III)

For planet (B): Mass $= \dfrac{M}{2}$, Radius $= 2R$
$v_B = \sqrt{\dfrac{2G\left(\dfrac{M}{2}\right)}{2R}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{4} \times \dfrac{2GM}{R}} = \dfrac{v_e}{2}$. (Matches II)

For planet (C): Mass $= 2M$, Radius $= 2R$
$v_C = \sqrt{\dfrac{2G(2M)}{2R}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}} = v_e$. (Matches I)

For planet (D): Mass $= 4M$, Radius $= \dfrac{R}{4}$
$v_D = \sqrt{\dfrac{2G(4M)}{\dfrac{R}{4}}} = \sqrt{16 \times \dfrac{2GM}{R}} = 4v_e$. (Matches IV)

Therefore, the correct matching is (A)-(III), (B)-(II), (C)-(I), (D)-(IV).

Answer: (A)-(III), (B)-(II), (C)-(I), (D)-(IV)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Velocity of projection from Earth's surface)List-II (Maximum height reached)
(A) $\dfrac{V_e}{\sqrt{2}}$(I) $\dfrac{R}{3}$
(B) $\dfrac{V_e}{2}$(II) $R$
(C) $\dfrac{\sqrt{3}V_e}{2}$(III) $2R$
(D) $\sqrt{\dfrac{2}{3}}V_e$(IV) $3R$

($V_e$ is the escape velocity and $R$ is the radius of the Earth)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
Let the velocity of projection be $v = k V_e$. By conservation of mechanical energy:

$\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 - \dfrac{GMm}{R} = -\dfrac{GMm}{R+h}$

Since $V_e = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}}$, we have $v^2 = k^2 \dfrac{2GM}{R}$.

$\dfrac{1}{2}m\left(k^2 \dfrac{2GM}{R}\right) - \dfrac{GMm}{R} = -\dfrac{GMm}{R+h}$

$\dfrac{GMm}{R}(k^2 - 1) = -\dfrac{GMm}{R+h}$

$R+h = \dfrac{R}{1-k^2} \Rightarrow h = \dfrac{Rk^2}{1-k^2}$

(A) For $v = \dfrac{V_e}{\sqrt{2}}$, $k = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \Rightarrow h = \dfrac{R(1/2)}{1 - 1/2} = R$

(B) For $v = \dfrac{V_e}{2}$, $k = \dfrac{1}{2} \Rightarrow h = \dfrac{R(1/4)}{1 - 1/4} = \dfrac{R}{3}$

(C) For $v = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}V_e}{2}$, $k = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \Rightarrow h = \dfrac{R(3/4)}{1 - 3/4} = 3R$

(D) For $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2}{3}}V_e$, $k = \sqrt{\dfrac{2}{3}} \Rightarrow h = \dfrac{R(2/3)}{1 - 2/3} = 2R$

Thus, the correct matching is (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(III).

Answer: (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(III)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A hypothetical planet has an acceleration due to gravity at its surface that is $4$ times that of the Earth, and its radius is half that of the Earth. If the escape velocity on the surface of the Earth is $v_e$, what is the escape velocity on the surface of this hypothetical planet?
questions.solution:
The escape velocity $v$ on the surface of a planet is related to its acceleration due to gravity $g$ and radius $R$ by the formula $v = \sqrt{2gR}$.

For the Earth, $v_e = \sqrt{2g_e R_e}$.

For the hypothetical planet, the acceleration due to gravity is $g_p = 4g_e$ and the radius is $R_p = \dfrac{R_e}{2}$.

The escape velocity on the planet is:
$v_p = \sqrt{2g_p R_p}$

Substituting the given values:
$v_p = \sqrt{2(4g_e)\left(\dfrac{R_e}{2}\right)} = \sqrt{4(g_e R_e)} = \sqrt{2} \sqrt{2g_e R_e} = \sqrt{2} v_e$.

Thus, the escape velocity on the hypothetical planet is $\sqrt{2} v_e$.

Answer: $\sqrt{2} v_e$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle is projected vertically upwards from the surface of the Earth such that it reaches a maximum height equal to three times the radius of the Earth ($3R$). If $V_e$ is the escape velocity on the surface of the Earth, the initial velocity of projection of the particle is
questions.solution:
Let the mass of the Earth be $M$, radius be $R$, and mass of the particle be $m$.

By conservation of mechanical energy between the surface of the Earth and the maximum height:
$K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f$

At the surface, the distance from the center of the Earth is $R$. At the maximum height $h = 3R$, the distance from the center is $r = R + 3R = 4R$.

$\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 - \dfrac{GMm}{R} = 0 - \dfrac{GMm}{4R}$

$\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = \dfrac{GMm}{R} - \dfrac{GMm}{4R} = \dfrac{3GMm}{4R}$

We know that the escape velocity $V_e = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}}$, which gives $\dfrac{GM}{R} = \dfrac{V_e^2}{2}$.

Substituting this into the energy equation:
$\dfrac{1}{2}v^2 = \dfrac{3}{4} \left( \dfrac{V_e^2}{2} \right)$

$v^2 = \dfrac{3}{4} V_e^2$

$v = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} V_e$

Answer: $\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} V_e$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two planets $A$ and $B$ have the same uniform mass density. The radius of planet $A$ is three times the radius of planet $B$. If $v_A$ and $v_B$ are the escape velocities on the surfaces of planets $A$ and $B$ respectively, then the ratio $\dfrac{v_A}{v_B}$ is :
questions.solution:
The escape velocity on the surface of a planet is given by $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}}$.

Since the mass of a planet is $M = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^3 \rho$, where $\rho$ is the uniform mass density, we can write:

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2G}{R} \left(\dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^3 \rho\right)} = R\sqrt{\dfrac{8\pi G \rho}{3}}$

For planets with the same uniform density, the escape velocity is directly proportional to the radius ($v \propto R$).

Therefore, the ratio of their escape velocities is:

$\dfrac{v_A}{v_B} = \dfrac{R_A}{R_B}$

Given that $R_A = 3R_B$, we have:

$\dfrac{v_A}{v_B} = 3$

Answer: $3$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two hypothetical planets A and B have the same average mass density, but the radius of planet A is twice that of planet B. Two satellites revolve very close to the surfaces of their respective planets. The ratio of the time periods of the satellites of planet A to planet B is
questions.solution:
For a satellite orbiting very close to the surface of a planet, the orbital radius $r$ is approximately equal to the radius of the planet $R$ ($r \approx R$).

The time period of a satellite is given by:
$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{r^3}{GM}}$

Substituting $r = R$ and the mass of the planet $M = \text{Volume} \times \text{Density} = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^3 \rho$:
$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{R^3}{G \left(\dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^3 \rho\right)}}$

$T = \sqrt{\dfrac{3\pi}{G\rho}}$

This expression shows that the time period of a satellite orbiting close to the surface of a planet depends only on the density $\rho$ of the planet and is independent of its radius $R$.

Since planets A and B have the same average density ($\rho_A = \rho_B$), their satellites will have the same time period.

Therefore, the ratio of their time periods $T_A : T_B$ is $1:1$.

Answer: $1:1$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: For various planets in the solar system, a graph is plotted with the logarithm of the orbital time period ($\log T$) on the y-axis and the logarithm of the orbital radius ($\log r$) on the x-axis. What will be the slope of the resulting straight line?
questions.solution:
According to Kepler's Third Law of planetary motion, the square of the time period ($T$) of a planet is directly proportional to the cube of its orbital radius ($r$).

$T^2 = k r^3$

Taking the logarithm on both sides:
$\log(T^2) = \log(k r^3)$
$2 \log T = 3 \log r + \log k$

Rearranging the equation to match the form of a straight line ($y = mx + c$):
$\log T = \dfrac{3}{2} \log r + \dfrac{1}{2} \log k$

Here, $y = \log T$ and $x = \log r$. The slope of the graph ($m$) is the coefficient of $\log r$, which is $\dfrac{3}{2}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{3}{2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A body is projected vertically upwards from the surface of the Earth with an initial velocity exactly equal to the orbital velocity of a satellite revolving very close to the Earth's surface. The maximum height reached by the body is ($R$ is the radius of the Earth):
questions.solution:
The orbital velocity of a satellite revolving very close to the Earth's surface is given by $v_o = \sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{R}}$.

Let the maximum height reached by the body be $h$. Applying the principle of conservation of mechanical energy between the surface of the Earth and the maximum height:

$\dfrac{1}{2}mv_o^2 - \dfrac{GMm}{R} = -\dfrac{GMm}{R+h}$

Substituting $v_o^2 = \dfrac{GM}{R}$:

$\dfrac{1}{2}m\left(\dfrac{GM}{R}\right) - \dfrac{GMm}{R} = -\dfrac{GMm}{R+h}$

$-\dfrac{GMm}{2R} = -\dfrac{GMm}{R+h}$

$R+h = 2R$

$h = R$

Using the constant gravity approximation ($mgh = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2$) incorrectly yields $h = \dfrac{R}{2}$, and forgetting to subtract $R$ from the final distance yields $2R$.

Answer: $R$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Two unequal point masses $M_1$ and $M_2$ ($M_1 \gt M_2$) are separated by a distance $d$. Point $P$ is the neutral point (where the net gravitational field is zero) on the line segment joining them. Consider the following statements regarding point $P$:
(A) $P$ is closer to $M_2$.
(B) The net gravitational potential is zero at $P$.
(C) The magnitude of gravitational potential is minimum at $P$ compared to other points on the line segment between the masses.
(D) A particle placed at $P$ is in stable equilibrium along the line joining the masses.

How many of the above statements are correct?
questions.solution:
Statement (A) is correct: The neutral point occurs where the gravitational fields from both masses are equal in magnitude. Since $M_1 \gt M_2$, the point must be closer to the lighter mass $M_2$ to compensate for its smaller mass.

Statement (B) is incorrect: Gravitational potential due to a point mass is always negative. The net potential is the scalar sum of two negative values, so it can never be zero.

Statement (C) is correct: The gravitational field is the negative gradient of the potential ($E = -dV/dx$). At the neutral point, $E = 0$, so the potential $V$ has a local extremum. Since $d^2V/dx^2 \lt 0$, $V$ is a local maximum (least negative). Therefore, its magnitude $|V|$ is a local minimum.

Statement (D) is incorrect: For stable equilibrium, the potential energy $U$ must be a local minimum. Since $U = mV$ and $V$ is a local maximum at $P$, $U$ is also a local maximum. Thus, the equilibrium is unstable along the line joining the masses.

Therefore, exactly two statements are correct.

Answer: Only two

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A geostationary satellite orbits the Earth at a radial distance $R_G$ from the Earth's centre. Another artificial satellite orbits the Earth in a circular orbit of radius $\dfrac{R_G}{4}$. What is the time period of this second satellite?
questions.solution:
The time period of a geostationary satellite is $T_1 = 24 \text{ hours}$.

According to Kepler's Third Law, the square of the time period is proportional to the cube of the orbital radius, i.e., $T^2 \propto r^3$.

For the two satellites, we can write:
$\left(\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}\right)^2 = \left(\dfrac{r_2}{r_1}\right)^3$

Taking the square root on both sides:
$\dfrac{T_2}{T_1} = \left(\dfrac{r_2}{r_1}\right)^{3/2}$

Given $r_1 = R_G$ and $r_2 = \dfrac{R_G}{4}$:
$\dfrac{T_2}{24} = \left(\dfrac{R_G / 4}{R_G}\right)^{3/2} = \left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^{3/2} = \dfrac{1}{8}$

$T_2 = \dfrac{24}{8} = 3 \text{ hours}$.

questions.q: Two point masses $m$ and $4m$ are separated by an unknown distance $r$. The gravitational potential at the point on the line joining them where the net gravitational field is zero, is found to be $-V_0$. The separation distance $r$ between the two masses is:
questions.solution:
Let the neutral point (where the net gravitational field is zero) be at a distance $x$ from the mass $m$.

Equating the magnitudes of the gravitational fields produced by both masses at this point:
$\dfrac{Gm}{x^2} = \dfrac{G(4m)}{(r-x)^2}$

Taking the square root on both sides:
$\dfrac{1}{x} = \dfrac{2}{r-x}$
$\Rightarrow r - x = 2x \Rightarrow x = \dfrac{r}{3}$

The distance of this neutral point from the mass $4m$ is $r - \dfrac{r}{3} = \dfrac{2r}{3}$.

The net gravitational potential $V$ at this point is the scalar sum of the potentials due to both masses:
$V = -\dfrac{Gm}{x} - \dfrac{G(4m)}{r-x}$
$V = -\dfrac{Gm}{\left(\dfrac{r}{3}\right)} - \dfrac{4Gm}{\left(\dfrac{2r}{3}\right)}$
$V = -\dfrac{3Gm}{r} - \dfrac{6Gm}{r} = -\dfrac{9Gm}{r}$

We are given that the potential at this point is $-V_0$. Therefore:
$-V_0 = -\dfrac{9Gm}{r}$
$\Rightarrow r = \dfrac{9Gm}{V_0}$

Answer: $\dfrac{9Gm}{V_0}$

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Final position of mass $m$ initially at Earth's surface)List-II (Change in gravitational potential energy, $\Delta U$)
(A) Height $h = R$(I) $mgR$
(B) Height $h = 3R$(II) $0.5 mgR$
(C) Infinity(III) $0.75 mgR$
(D) Depth $d = \dfrac{R}{2}$(IV) $-0.375 mgR$

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
The change in gravitational potential energy when a mass $m$ is raised to a height $h$ from the Earth's surface is $\Delta U = \dfrac{mgh}{1 + \dfrac{h}{R}}$.

For (A) $h = R$:
$\Delta U = \dfrac{mgR}{1 + 1} = 0.5 mgR$. So, (A) matches with (II).

For (B) $h = 3R$:
$\Delta U = \dfrac{mg(3R)}{1 + 3} = \dfrac{3}{4} mgR = 0.75 mgR$. So, (B) matches with (III).

For (C) Infinity ($h \to \infty$):
$\Delta U = mgR$. So, (C) matches with (I).

For (D) Depth $d = \dfrac{R}{2}$:
The potential energy at depth $d$ is $U_d = -\dfrac{GMm}{2R^3}(3R^2 - r^2)$, where $r = R - d = \dfrac{R}{2}$.
$U_d = -\dfrac{GMm}{2R^3}\left(3R^2 - \dfrac{R^2}{4}\right) = -\dfrac{11}{8} \dfrac{GMm}{R} = -1.375 mgR$.
The potential energy at the surface is $U_s = -\dfrac{GMm}{R} = -mgR$.
$\Delta U = U_d - U_s = -1.375 mgR - (-mgR) = -0.375 mgR$. So, (D) matches with (IV).

The correct matching is (A) → (II), (B) → (III), (C) → (I), (D) → (IV).

Answer: (A) → (II), (B) → (III), (C) → (I), (D) → (IV)

questions.q: A student incorrectly uses the approximate formula $g' = g\left(1 - \dfrac{2h}{R}\right)$ to calculate the acceleration due to gravity at a height $h$ above the earth's surface (where $R$ is the radius of the earth). At a particular height, this formula predicts that the weight of a body will become zero. What is the true weight of the body at this height, if its weight on the surface of the earth is $W$?
questions.solution:
The approximate formula for acceleration due to gravity at a height $h$ is $g' = g\left(1 - \dfrac{2h}{R}\right)$.

According to the question, this formula predicts zero weight, so $g' = 0$.

$1 - \dfrac{2h}{R} = 0 \implies h = \dfrac{R}{2}$

The true acceleration due to gravity at a height $h$ is given by the exact formula:

$g_h = \dfrac{g}{\left(1 + \dfrac{h}{R}\right)^2}$

Substituting $h = \dfrac{R}{2}$:

$g_h = \dfrac{g}{\left(1 + \dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2} = \dfrac{g}{\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)^2} = \dfrac{4g}{9}$

Therefore, the true weight of the body is $W_{true} = m g_h = \dfrac{4}{9} mg = \dfrac{4W}{9}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{4W}{9}$

Given, Escape velocity on the surface of earth, $\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{e}}=11.1 \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{h}$
i.e.
$\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{e}}=\sqrt{2 \mathrm{gR}_{\mathrm{e}}} \\
& \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{e}}=\sqrt{\frac{2 \mathrm{GM}_{\mathrm{e}}}{\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{e}}}}
\end{aligned}$
Mass of moon, $M_m=\frac{M_e}{81}$
Radius of moon, $\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{m}}=\frac{\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{e}}}{4}\therefore$ Escape velocity on the surface of moon
$\begin{aligned}
& v_m=\sqrt{\frac{2 G M_m}{R_m}}=\sqrt{\frac{2 G \frac{M e}{81}}{\frac{R_e}{4}}} \\
& =\frac{2 \sqrt{2}}{9} \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{GM}_{\mathrm{c}}}{\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{c}}}}=\frac{2}{9} \sqrt{\frac{2 \mathrm{GM}_{\mathrm{c}}}{\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{c}}}}=\frac{2}{9} \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{e}}=\frac{2}{9} \times 11.1=2.46 \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{h} \end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: At what distance (in metre) from the centre of the Moon, the intensity of gravitational field will be zero? (Take, mass of Earth and Moon as $5.98 \times 10^{24} \mathrm{~kg}$ and $7.35 \times 10^{22} \mathrm{~kg}$ respectively and the distance between Moon and Earth is $3.85 \times 10^8 \mathrm{~m}$.)
questions.solution:
Let X be the distance of the point from the centre of earth where gravitational intensity is zero. Therefore,
$\frac{\mathrm{GM}_{\mathrm{e}}}{\mathrm{x}^2}=\frac{\mathrm{GM}_{\mathrm{m}}}{\left(3.85 \times 10^8-\mathrm{x}\right)^2}$
or $\frac{\mathrm{x}}{3.85 \times 10^8-\mathrm{x}}=\sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{e}}}{\mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{m}}}}=\sqrt{\frac{5.98 \times 10^{24}}{7.35 \times 10^{22}}} \cong 9$
or $\quad \frac{x}{9}+x=3.85 \times 10^8$
or $\quad \mathrm{x}=9 \times 3.85 \times 10^8 / 10=3.46 \times 10^8 \mathrm{~m}$
Distance from Moon $=3.85 \times 10^8-3.46 \times 10^8=3.9 \times 10^7 \mathrm{~m} \cong 3.85 \times 10^7 \mathrm{~m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: R is the radius of Earth and $\omega$ is its angular velocity and $g_p$ is the value of $g$ at the poles. The effective value of $g$ at a latitude $\lambda=60^{\circ}$.
questions.solution:
The acceleration due to gravity at a latitude $\lambda$ is
$\mathrm{g}^{\prime}=\mathrm{g}-\mathrm{R} \omega^2 \cos ^2 \lambda$
At the poles, $\lambda=90^{\circ}\therefore \quad \mathrm{g}^{\prime}=\mathrm{g}=\mathrm{g}_{\mathrm{p}}$
For $\quad \lambda=60^{\circ}$,
$\mathrm{g}^{\prime}=\mathrm{g}_{\mathrm{p}}-\mathrm{R} \omega^2 \cos ^2 \lambda$
or $\quad g^{\prime}=g_p-R \omega^2 \cos ^2 60^{\circ}=g_p-R \omega^2\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2=g_p-\frac{1}{4} R \omega^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A rocket is intended to leave the Earth's gravitational field. The fuel in its main engine is a little less than the amount that is necessary and an auxiliary engine, (only capable of operating for a short time) has to be used as well. When is it best to switch on the auxiliary engine?
options: when the rocket has nearly stopped with respect to the Earth.
questions.solution:
The rocket has to reach the highest possible total energy. If the zero level of gravitational potential energy is 'infinitely' far away, then the energy of the rocket standing on the surface of the earth is negative. The energy released during the operation of the engines increases the total energy of the rocket, and the rocket can leave, the earth's gravitational field if the sum of its potential and kinetic energies becomes positive.
The energy released in the course of the operation of the principal and auxiliary engines increases the total energy of the rocket and its ejected combustion products by a fixed value; this increase is independent of the moment when the engines are scratched on. However, the speed at which the combustion products fall back to the earth does depend on the timing of the rocket's operations. Indeed, if the auxiliary engine starts working when the rocket is at a greater height, the combustion products fall further and their speed and total energy are higher when they hit the ground. This means that the sooner the auxiliary engine is switched on, the higher the energy ultimately acquired by the rocket. The same argument is valid for the principal engine, and if the only energy consideration apply, it is best to operate the engines for the shortest time and at the highest thrust.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The planets with radii $R_1$ and $R_2$ have densities $\rho_1, \quad \rho_2$ respectively. Their atmospheric pressures are $p_1$ and $p_2$ respectively. Therefore, the ratio of masses of their atmospheres, neglecting variation of $g$ within the limits of atmosphere is
questions.solution:
Acceleration due to gravity,
$\begin{aligned}
& g=\frac{G M}{R^2}=\frac{4}{3} \pi \rho G R \\
& \therefore \frac{g_1}{g_2}=\frac{\rho_1 R_1}{\rho_2 R_2}
\end{aligned}$
Atmospheric pressure can be given by $p=\frac{W}{S}$
where, $W=$ Weight of atmosphere,
$S=$ Surface area of the planet
$\therefore \frac{m_1}{m_2}=\frac{\rho_1 S_1 g_2}{\rho_2 S_2 g_1}=\frac{p_1 \cdot\left(4 \pi R_1^2\right)}{p_2\left(4 \pi R_2^2\right)} \cdot \frac{\rho_2 R_1}{\rho_1 R_1}=\frac{p_1 R_1 \rho_2}{p_2 R_2 \rho_1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A body of mass $2 m$ is placed on earth's surface. Calculate the change in gravitational potential energy, if this body is taken from earth's surface to a height of $h$, where $h=4 R$.
questions.solution:
Potential energy, $U=-\frac{G M m}{r}=\frac{-2 G M m}{r} \quad[\because m=2 m]$
At earth's surface, $r=R\therefore \quad U_e=-\frac{2 G M m}{R}$
Now, if a body is taken to height, $h=4 R$, then the potential energy is given by
$\begin{aligned} U_h & =-\frac{2 G M m}{R+h} \quad[\because r=h+R] \\ & =\frac{-2 G M m}{5 R}\end{aligned}$
Thus, change in gravitational potential energy,
$\begin{aligned} \Delta U & =U_h-U_e \\ & =-\frac{2 G M m}{5 R}+\frac{2 G M m}{R}=\frac{8}{5} \frac{G M m}{R}\end{aligned}\begin{aligned} \therefore \quad \Delta U & =\frac{8}{5} \frac{g R^2 m}{R} \quad\left[\because G M=g R^2\right] \\ & =\frac{8}{5} m g R\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniform ring of mass $m$ and radius $a$ is placed directly above a uniform sphere of mass $M$ and of equal to radius. The centre of the ring is at a distance $\sqrt{3} a$ from the centre of the sphere. The gravitational force $(F)$ exerted by the sphere on the ring is
questions.solution: Now, the gravitational field due to the ring at a distance $d=\sqrt{3} a$ on its axis is $E=\frac{G m d}{\left(a^2+d^2\right)^{3 / 2}}=\frac{\sqrt{3} G m}{8 a^2}$ The force in a particle of mass $M$ placed here is $F=M E=\frac{\sqrt{3} G M m}{8 a^2}$ This is also the force due to the sphere in the ring.

questions.q: Change in acceleration due to gravity is same upto a height $h$ from each other the earth surface and below depth $x$, then relation between $x$ and $h$ is ( $h$ and $x\lt\lt \lt R_e$ )
questions.solution:
Variation in $g$ at a height $h$ from the earth surface $g^{\prime}=g\left(1-\frac{2 h}{R_e}\right)$
Variation in $g$ at a depth $x$ below the earth surface $g^{\prime \prime}=g\left(1-\frac{x}{R_b}\right)$
But variations are same
$\therefore \quad g\left(1-\frac{2 h}{R_\theta}\right)=g\left(1-\frac{x}{R_\theta}\right)\therefore \quad x=2 h$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The escape velocity for the earth is $11.2 \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{s}$. The mass of another planet 100 times mass of earth and its radius is 4 times radius of the earth. The escape velocity for the planet is
questions.solution:
The escape velocity of the the planet
$\begin{aligned} v_{\text {escape }} & =\sqrt{\frac{2 G m}{R}} \propto \sqrt{\frac{M}{R}} \\ \frac{v_p}{v_e} & =\sqrt{\frac{M_p}{R_p} \times \frac{R_e}{M_e}} \\ \frac{v_p}{v_e} & =\sqrt{100 \times \frac{1}{4}}=5 \\ v_p & =5 \times 11.2=56 \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{s}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A satellite orbiting the earth in a circular orbit of radius $R$ completes one revolution in 3h. If orbital radius of geostationary satellite is 36000 km , orbital radius of earth is
questions.solution:
Time period of satellite
$T^2=\frac{4 \pi^2}{G M} r^3 \text { or } T^2=\frac{4 \pi^2}{g R^2} r^3 \quad\left[\because G M=g R^2\right]$
or $\quad T=\frac{2 \pi}{R} \sqrt{\frac{r^3}{g}}$ or $T \propto r^{3 / 2}\therefore \quad \frac{T_1}{T_2}=\left(\frac{r_1}{r_2}\right)^{3 / 2}$
Given, $\quad T_1=3 \mathrm{~h}, T_2=24 \mathrm{~h}$ (geostationary
satellite) $r_1=R, r_2=36000 \mathrm{~km}\therefore \quad \frac{3}{24}=\left(\frac{R}{36000}\right)^{3 / 2}$
or $\quad R=\left(\frac{1}{8}\right)^{2 / 3} \times 36000$ or $\quad R=\frac{1}{4} \times 36000=9000 \mathrm{~km}$

questions.q: Two spherical bodies of masses $M$ and $5 M$ and radii $R$ and $2 R$ respectively are released in free space with initial separation between their centres equal to $12 R$. If they attract each other due to gravitational force only,then the distance covered by the smaller body just before collision, is
questions.solution: Let at $O$ there will be a collision. If smaller sphere moves $x$ distance to reach at $O$, then bigger sphere will move a distance of $(9 R-x)$. $\begin{aligned} F & =\frac{G M \times 5 M}{(12 R-x)^2} \\ a_{\text {small }} & =\frac{F}{M}=\frac{G \times 5 M}{(12 R-x)^2} \\ a_{\mathrm{big}} & =\frac{F}{5 M}=\frac{G M}{(12 R-x)^2} \\ x & =\frac{1}{2} a_{\text {small }} t^2=\frac{1}{2} \frac{G \times 5 M}{(12 R-x)^2} t^2 \ldots(i)\\ (9 R-x) & =\frac{1}{2} a_{\text {big }} t^2=\frac{1}{2} \frac{G M}{(12 R-x)^2} t^2\ldots(ii) \end{aligned}$ Thus, dividing Eq. (i) by Eq. (ii), we get $\frac{x}{9 R-x}=5\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \quad x=45 R-5 x \\ & \Rightarrow \quad 6 x=45 R \\ & \therefore \quad x=7.5 R \\ & \end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A launching vehicle carrying an artificial satellite of mass $m$ is set for launch on the surface of the earth of mass $M$ and radius $R$. If the satellite is intended to move in a circular orbit of radius $7 R$, the minimum energy required to be spent by the launching vehicle on the satellite is (Gravitational constant $=G$ )
questions.solution:
The energy of artificial satellite at the surface of the earth
$E_1=-\frac{G M m}{R}$
When the satellite is intended to move in a circular orbit of radius $7 R$, then energy of artificial satellite
$E_2=-\frac{1}{2} \frac{G M m}{7 R}$
The minimum energy required
$E=E_1-E_2=-\frac{G M m}{R}+\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{G M m}{7 R}\right)=\frac{-14 G M m+G M m}{14 R}=-\frac{13 G M m}{14 R}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two satellites of earth, $S_1$ and $S_2$, are moving in the same orbit. The mass of $S_1$ is four times the mass of $S_2$. Which one of the following statements is true?
options: The time period of $S_1$ is four times that of $S_2$
The potential energies of earth and satellite in the two cases are equal
$S_1$ and $S_2$ are moving with the same speed
The kinetic energies of the two satellites are equal
questions.solution:
When two satellites of earth are moving in same orbit, then time period of both are equal. From Kepler's third law
$T^2 \propto r^3$
Time period is independent of mass, hence their time periods will be equal.
The potential energy and kinetic energy are mass dependent, hence the PE and KE of satellites are not equal.
But, if they are orbiting in a same orbit, then they have equal orbital speed.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: For a satellite moving in an orbit around the earth, the ratio of kinetic energy to potential energy is
questions.solution:
Key Idea : Kinetic energy of satellite is half of its potential energy.
Potential energy of satellite
$U=-\frac{G M_e m}{R_e}$
where $R_e$ is radius of earth, $M_e$ the mass of earth, $m$ the mass of satellite and $G$ the gravitational constant.
$|U|=\frac{G M_e m}{R_e}$
Kinetic energy of satellite
$K=\frac{1}{2} \frac{G M_e m}{R_e}$
Thus,$\frac{K}{|U|}=\frac{1}{2} \frac{G M_e m}{R_e} \times \frac{R_e}{G M_e m}=\frac{1}{2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The speed of earth's rotation about its axis is $\omega$. Its speed is increased to $x$ times to make the effective acceleration due to gravity equal to zero at the equator. Then $x$ is
questions.solution:
Earth rotates about its own axis in 24 h .
So, $\quad T=24 \times 60 \times 60 \mathrm{~s}$
So, angular speed of earth about its own axis
$\omega=\frac{2 \pi}{T}=\frac{2 \pi}{24 \times 60 \times 60} \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s}$
At equator, $g^{\prime}=g-R_e \omega^{\prime 2}$
or $\quad 0=g-R_e \omega^{\prime 2}$
or $\omega^{\prime}=\sqrt{\frac{g}{R_e}}=\frac{2 \pi}{84.6 \times 60}\therefore \quad \frac{\omega^{\prime}}{\omega}=\frac{24 \times 60 \times 60}{84.6 \times 60} \approx 17\Rightarrow \quad \omega^{\prime}=17 \omega$
So, value of $x$ is 17 .

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Imagine a new planet having the same density as that of earth but it is $3$ times bigger than the earth in size. If the acceleration due to gravity on the surface of earth is $g$ and that on the surface of the new planet is $g^{\prime}$, then
questions.solution:
The acceleration due to gravity on the new planet can be found using the relation $g=\frac{G M}{R^2}...(i)$
but $M=\frac{4}{3} \pi R^3 \rho, \rho$ being density.
Thus, Eq. (i) becomes
$\therefore  g=\frac{G \times \frac{4}{3} \pi R^3 \rho}{R^2}=G \times \frac{4}{3} \pi R \rho\begin{array}{ll}\Rightarrow & g \propto R \\ \therefore & \frac{g^{\prime}}{g}=\frac{R^{\prime}}{R} \\ \Rightarrow & \frac{g^{\prime}}{g}=\frac{3 R}{R}=3 \\ \Rightarrow & g^{\prime}=3 g\end{array}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Earth is revolving around the sun. If the distance of the earth from the sun is reduced to $1 / 4$ th of the present distance then the length of present day will be reduced by :
questions.solution:
From Kepler's law
$\begin{aligned} & T^2 \propto R^3 \\ & \therefore \quad\left(\frac{T_1}{T_2}\right)^2=\left(\frac{R_1}{R_2}\right)^3 \\ & \frac{T_1}{T_2}=\left(\frac{R_1}{R_2}\right)^{3 / 2}=\left(\frac{R}{R / 4}\right)^{3 / 2} \\ & =(4)^{3 / 2}=(2)^3=8 \\ & \therefore \quad T_2=\frac{T_1}{8} \\ & \end{aligned}$
Hence, the length of the day is reduced by $\frac{1}{8}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: There are two planets and the ratio of radius of the two planets is $K$ but ratio of acceleration due to gravity of both planets is $g$. What will be the ratio of their escape velocity?
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} v_e & =\sqrt{R g} \\ \frac{v_1}{v_2} & =\sqrt{\frac{R_1}{R_2} \cdot \frac{g_1}{g_2}} \\ & =\sqrt{K g} \\ & =(K g)^{1 / 2}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Radius of orbit of satellite of earth is $R$. Its kinetic energy is proportional to
questions.solution:
Kinetic energy of the satellite
$\mathrm{KE}=\frac{1}{2} m v_0^2$ ...(1)
where $v_0=\sqrt{\frac{G M}{R}}$
Now putting the value of $v_0$ is eq. (1), we get
$\mathrm{KE}=\frac{1}{2} m\left(\sqrt{\frac{G M}{R}}\right)^2=\frac{1}{2} \frac{m G M}{R}$
Hence, $\mathrm{KE} \propto \frac{1}{R}$
